Executive Summary

This portfolio has recovered $370.62 of $60,793.68 placed — a liquidation rate of 0.61%. Two accounts have resolved: Pierce, T. ($195.10), Tantra Brew House ($175.52). The remaining $77,729.78 open balance is spread across 84 accounts averaging $925.35.

Across 86 placed accounts, Southwest Recovery Services has logged 11,597 individual collection actions since 04/20/2023: 5,024 outbound call attempts (3,028 ending in a voicemail or delivered message), 5,839 emails, 517 collection letters, 84 validation notices, 74 skip-trace actions, 47 text messages and 8 inbound contacts.

The open balance is $18,606.72 higher than the amount originally placed on those accounts because of balance updates recorded after placement. Individual account activity, the numbers on file and the note log are available by expanding any account in the Account Detail section below.

What Shaped the Results

We reviewed the 302 documents you uploaded to the portal (invoices, placement files and summaries), the numbers on file, and the complete account note trail (17,911 notes; 17,030 after exact duplicates are removed). No single factor explains the result. The factors we can document are grouped by who controls them, so you can see what we will change, what we need from MI-BOX, and what sits with the debtors.

Outcome to date: $370.62 recovered of $60,793.68 placed (0.61%), on two accounts. Both accounts that resolved paid in full once the balance was clear and the debtor engaged: Pierce paid the full $195.10, and Tantra Brew House paid $175.52 after a $1,300 balance adjustment. A conversation with the debtor is documented on 11 of the 86 accounts.
1. How the portfolio was worked
  • Small balances, worked at scale. The average placed balance is $706.90, and the portfolio ran through automated multi-channel campaigns: 5,024 call attempts (4,437 AI, 404 dialer, 183 collector), 5,839 emails, 517 collection letters, 47 texts and 74 skip-trace searches. Collectors wrote 136 notes on 66 accounts; 20 accounts have no collector note.
  • Contact was the constraint. That volume produced 8 inbound contacts in more than three years.
  • Contact data was thin, and in places wrong. The placement files give one phone number per placement (88% in the “Other Phone” field) and flag bounced emails on 23 of 180 rows and delivery-site addresses on 13. We will suppress every flagged email and address from day one.
  • Documents were not tied to debtors. Uploads sit on your client account, not on each debtor, and each monthly invoice became its own account (35 accounts for 13 debtors, each with its own letters and emails).
  • What we needed was not in the file. Signed agreements, who signed, the card on file and container status were not part of the placements. The checklist below lists each item and why it changes the outcome.
2. What the placement files contained
  • Thin placement files. One phone number per placement (88% in the “Other Phone” field), no date of birth or SSN on any of the 180 placement rows, and an account number on 3%.
  • Late placement. Accounts reached us a median of about 140 days after the invoice was due, and 43 of the 111 invoices we have were over 180 days old. Industry benchmark data puts the chance of collecting at about 69% at three months past due, 51% at six, 21% at twelve and 9% at twenty-four. These are benchmarks, not a promise.
  • Few documents. We have one executed agreement for 63 debtors, and a written summary for 5 of them.
  • Declined cards. 39 of the 111 invoices we have note a card on file that was declined or could not be charged.
3. The debtors’
  • Not responding. 3,028 call attempts ended in a voicemail or delivered message. Only 8 inbound contacts were recorded in more than three years.
  • Disputes we could not answer. Some debtors say they never signed or contest damage charges. Without the signed agreement and evidence we could not resolve them.
  • Contact stopped. Two accounts are in Cease and Desist at the debtor’s request and one was removed at your direction.

Signed Agreements vs. Invoices

We received invoices for 24 of your 63 debtors (111 invoices totaling $37,577.90), your placement spreadsheet for every account, and one executed agreement (a storage agreement signed in 2019). The agreement sets late fees at $15 after 10 days and $25 after 30 days, and a billing sheet describes a further $25 for each month past due.

Invoice typeInvoicesAmountWhat the invoices show
Monthly container rent (recurring)94$27,413.95Late-fee lines total $7,985.00 (29% of these invoices). On 35 of them the late fees exceed half of the base rent charge.
One-time invoices (repairs, pickups, cleaning, damage)17$10,163.95No photos or work orders came with them. Three of the monthly invoices also carry a pickup or damage line ($929.46).
This explains some of the resistance we meet. Debtors may pay or accept the rent and contest the late fees and damage charges, and we cannot answer a dispute without the signed agreement and evidence. Separating rent, late fees and damages on each invoice makes every balance easier to explain.

What Was Left Out of the Placements, and What It Costs

A placement file is the raw material for everything we can say and do. This table shows what the files did not carry, what that did to collectability, and what changes when it is provided.

Left outWhat the files showEffect on collectabilityWith it, we can
Signed agreement, and who signed itOne executed agreement for 63 debtorsDebtors who say they never signed or dispute charges cannot be answered, and one dispute can stop an account. Notices cannot cite your own late-fee or fee terms.Cite your agreement’s terms in the notice, answer disputes with the document, and give your attorney the contract for fee claims.
Legal entity, owner or guarantor (business accounts)Not in the files. 11 debtors look like businesses by nameNotices go to a trade name or the wrong party, and an owner cannot be pursued without a signature or guarantee.Run the business workup (entity status, owners and officers, liens, lawsuits, bankruptcy) and address the right party with the right authority.
Individual or business, and how the container was usedNot marked on the placementsThe wrong notice track and the wrong rules apply, because consumer notices and commercial demands are different.Send the consumer series or the commercial demand series, each with its matching Texas statute block and payment link.
Invoice due dates, one ledger per debtor, account numberInvoices for 24 of 63 debtors. Each monthly invoice became its own account (35 accounts for 13 debtors). $18,606.72 added after placement. Account number on 3% of rowsBalances are hard to explain or defend, the age of each debt is unclear, payments are hard to match, and limitation dates cannot be set with confidence.One account per debtor with rent, late fees and damages separate. Days past due, interest and limitation dates calculated, and time-sensitive accounts sent to your attorney.
More than one phone numberOne per placement, 88% in the “Other Phone” field5,024 call attempts produced 8 inbound contacts. 3,028 ended in a voicemail or delivered message.Skip trace from a second contact and reach the debtor at a working number.
A working emailBounce flagged on 23 of 180 rowsEmail is the main channel in our series, and every bounce is a notice that never arrives.Put the weekly, rotating email series in front of someone who receives it.
Billing address, apart from the delivery address13 rows flagged as a delivery siteLetters go to a job site, and the state-specific legal block comes from the address.Mail to the right place and use the correct state’s statute language.
Date of birth, last four of license or SSN, or business tax IDNone on any of the 180 rowsWe cannot confirm we have the right person, match the account for credit reporting, or screen for bankruptcy, deceased and military status.Confirm identity, find debtors who moved, run the pre-contact screens, and match accounts for reporting.
Card on file result39 of 111 invoices note a declined cardThe fastest, cheapest recovery is not retried.Ask you for a retry, then follow up with the debtor.
Container status and damage evidenceNo photos or work orders on 17 one-time invoices ($10,163.95)Damage charges are the first thing disputed, and it is unclear whether rent is still building.Answer disputes with evidence, and stop rent building on a container that has been returned.
Settlement authority and your wordingNot providedSettlement and discount notices cannot go out, and every notice speaks in our voice, not yours.Offer the discounts you approve, with your name and message on every notice.
Placement within 30 daysMedian about 140 days after the due date. 43 of 111 invoices were over 180 days oldBenchmarks put the chance of collecting at about 69% at three months past due, 51% at six, 21% at twelve and 9% at twenty-four.A standing weekly file of everything unpaid at 30 days.
How the new templates and research tools use these items
  • A notice series built for MI-BOX. This month we built customized notice series for other clients, including a utility client and a business-services client. Each has its own sequence of notices, its own request page and payment link, and wording drawn from the client’s own agreement and website. MI-BOX would get its own, built from your lease, your site and your payment options.
  • A request page for debtors. Debtors can tell us they paid MI-BOX directly or ask for a copy of their agreement or statement. We stop contact on the ones who paid and send documents on request. It needs your agreement and statements.
  • Commercial demand series. Official-looking demand letters with a seven-day payment deadline, addressed to the legal entity, with a payment link that carries the company’s name and a Texas statute block taken from the official source. The notices cite statutes; case law goes to your attorney’s packet.
  • Legal research gateway. It pulls Texas statutes from the official source, checks every citation, and runs the business workup and the pre-contact screens.
  • Without your items, we cannot cite your contract, address the right party or owner, set limitation dates with confidence, or offer a settlement. With them, every notice carries your terms, your name and the right authority.

Priorities & Recommendations

1. Time-sensitive: review with your attorney now

Texas generally allows four years to sue on a debt (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.004). The dates below come from the oldest invoice due date in the files you uploaded, matched to debtors by name. Some are past four years and others reach it within about six months. Your attorney should confirm each date and which rule applies; open accounts between businesses, for example, accrue differently (§ 16.004(c)). Debtor balances include newer invoices that are not yet old. Whether any step is appropriate on these accounts is for you and your attorney to decide once the dates are confirmed.

2. Your rights as a creditor, and what we will prepare for your attorney
RightWhat it doesSource
Attorney’s feesFees can be added to the debt on claims for services, goods, sworn accounts and written contracts. Since 2021 they can be recovered from organizations as well as individuals. It takes an attorney, a presented claim, and 30 days without payment.Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 38.001–.002
Sworn accountWith an itemized, sworn account, the debtor generally has to file a sworn denial to dispute the charges. Without one, the account stands as proof.Tex. R. Civ. P. 185; Rizk v. Financial Guardian Ins. Agency, 584 S.W.2d 860 (Tex. 1979)
PresentmentThe demand that starts the 30-day period has no required form. Your attorney’s letter removes any doubt.Jones v. Kelley, 614 S.W.2d 95 (Tex. 1981)
Business accountsA company’s owner is generally not personally liable on its contract unless the owner signed or guaranteed it. This is why who signed matters.Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code § 21.223; Willis v. Donnelly, 199 S.W.3d 262 (Tex. 2006)
Your lease termsThe card charge after 30 days late and retrieval of the container are remedies under your own agreement. Whether any lien or sale process applies is for your attorney.Your agreement
This is information for MI-BOX, not legal advice, and SWRS does not file suit. Statute text was checked against the Texas Legislative Council site. Case citations were checked to confirm they exist, and your attorney should review whether each is still good law.
3. What we need from MI-BOX to succeed, and why each one matters
We needWhy it matters to collecting
Signed agreement for each debtor, and who signed itIt is the proof of what the debtor agreed to: rent, late charges, the card authorization. Without it, one dispute can stop an account. On business accounts it also shows who signed and whether a person, not just the company, is responsible.
Second phone, alternate contact, working emailWe received one phone number per debtor. When it fails, we have no other way to reach them. 23 of your 180 placement rows say the email bounces.
Billing address, apart from the delivery addressLetters and notices sent to a job site or delivery location never reach the debtor. Your files flagged 13. We cannot locate or confirm who we are dealing with from a delivery address.
Card on file: declined or not, and a retryThe agreement lets MI-BOX charge the card after 30 days late. It is the fastest, cheapest recovery. If it fails, it tells us what to expect. 39 of the invoices we have show a declined card.
Container status: on site, picked up, dateShows whether MI-BOX still holds the container and its contents, which is real leverage, and whether rent is still adding to the balance.
Damage evidence: photos, work orders, repair costDamage charges are the first thing debtors dispute ($10,163.95 on 17 one-time invoices). Evidence is what resolves a dispute and lets us keep working the account.
Payments received directly, and payment plansSo we never contact someone who has paid or is on a plan, and the balance we quote is right.
Short summary on your 15 largest accountsThe history that does not fit in a file: promises, conversations, disputes. A person can start at the right place, not from zero. We have a summary for only 5 of your 63 debtors.
One monthly file per debtor, with a ledgerSeparates rent, late fees and damages so a balance can be explained and defended, and puts one debtor on one account.
Identifiers, whatever you have: date of birth, last four of driver’s license or SSN, business tax ID, employerThese let us confirm we have the right person, find them when they move, check bankruptcy, deceased and military status before we contact anyone, and match the account for credit reporting. None of the 180 placement rows had a date of birth or SSN. Your agreement uses the last four of the driver’s license as the access PIN, so you may already have it.
Your ledger for the post-placement balance additionsYour portal uploads added 65 debit adjustments after placement ($18,606.72). We need your ledger to confirm each one, so every balance we quote ties to your books.
For each business account: legal entity name, owner or guarantor, billing addressShows who is responsible and where to send notices. Your attorney needs it for any demand or suit.
Why speed matters. Each month between the due date and placement lowers the chance of collecting, and missing contact details and identifiers make every one of those months worse. A standing weekly placement file of everything unpaid at 30 days would put accounts in front of us while they are most collectable.

Our Request: A 90-Day Second Opportunity

We are asking MI-BOX for one more opportunity on a different footing: named collectors on the larger accounts, new research tools, attorney-ready packets, and a short list of items from you.

What we bring
  • A notice series built for MI-BOX: your own sequence of notices, request page and payment link, with your lease terms and Texas statute language, built the way we just built them for other clients.
  • Screening before contact: bankruptcy, deceased, military and Cease and Desist status, and limitation dates from your invoices.
  • Business research: entity status, owners and officers, registered agent, lawsuits and liens on the business accounts.
  • Attorney-ready packets: itemized sworn-account ledgers and demand letters for your attorney’s review, with Texas citations checked.
  • One account per debtor, with rent, late fees and damages shown separately.
  • A named collector on every account over $1,000, and a one-page report every month.
What we ask of MI-BOX
  • The priority items above within 14 days: signed agreements and who signed, billing address and a second contact, card and container status, and a ledger per debtor.
  • A weekly placement file of everything unpaid at 30 days.
  • An attorney to receive the packets and decide on demand letters and suit.
  • A day-90 review against targets we set together in week 1.
The 90 days
WhenWhat happens
Week 1Flagged emails and addresses are suppressed. A named collector reviews every account over $1,000. Accounts are combined to one per debtor. Every account is screened for limitation dates, and the time-sensitive ones go to your attorney. We reconcile the $18,606.72 of post-placement additions with your ledger.
Days 8 to 30Using your items: locate debtors from the second contacts, research the business accounts and their owners, and reconcile every balance so rent, fees and damages are separate.
Day 30A ready list for your attorney: a card retry, a demand letter, retrieving a container, or a suit on the largest balances.
Every monthOne page, plain numbers: contacts made, promises, payments, accounts closed out, and what we still need from you.
Day 90Review together against the agreed targets. If they are not met, you decide what stays with us.
Will you give us the chance? 90 days, the items above, and a review at day 90. Our commitments from the day you agree: no automated contact on an account until a person has reviewed it; no new fees; and one named person you can call.

Methodology

Document review. We reviewed the 302 files MI-BOX uploaded to the client portal: 180 placement spreadsheet rows, 111 invoices, six client summaries and one executed agreement. Documents added by SWRS staff on individual debtor records are not included in these counts. Invoice and document counts are matched to debtors by name.

Data pulled live from the SWRS ADS collection system on October 28, 2026, covering all 86 accounts placed under Client Key 9292. Financial figures reconcile exactly to the Account Summary (DOR–DOA) report: $60,793.68 placed, $370.62 recovered, $77,729.78 open. Activity counts are derived from the complete account note log — 17,030 entries after removal of exact duplicates — together with dial records.

Southwest Recovery Services is a licensed and bonded collection agency. Collection of consumer accounts is subject to the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. § 1692 et seq.), Regulation F (12 C.F.R. Part 1006), the Texas Debt Collection Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. § 1681 et seq.). This report is information for MI-BOX and is not legal advice.

Activity log view: phone numbers show the last four digits, email addresses are partly masked, and debtor first names are shortened to an initial. System entries (failed sends and internal notifications) are not shown. The action counts in this report were computed before those entries were hidden.
